turns.content: so my brother marcus got the whole 36800 death benefit from dads job named beneficiary and i was the one doing everything 18 months straight no pay quitting my job burning my savings and he visited twice maybe 😅 i printed an invoice for 35000 based on what a home health aide would cost for 18 months and im gonna hand it to him at the probate meeting and tell him he morally owes me his entire half of the 28000 from the bank account to settle up do you think that makes sense or am i crazy for expecting him to give it all up

Based on what you describe, you provided 18 months of unpaid care and incurred lost income and savings. **That supports asking for a financial contribution; it does not, by itself, establish that Marcus owes you $35,000 or his entire inheritance from the bank account.**

Separate three issues:

- **The $36,800 death benefit:** A benefit paid to a named beneficiary generally passes outside probate. Being the beneficiary does not ordinarily make Marcus responsible for paying you for caregiving.
- **The $35,000 invoice:** A home-health-aide rate can help estimate the value of your work, but an invoice you create afterward does not itself establish a debt. Whether you have a claim against your dad’s estate depends on local law, any payment agreement, and other evidence. Lost wages, caregiving value, and actual expenses are different categories—not automatically reimbursable or additive.
- **The bank account:** If $28,000 is available for equal division between you, Marcus’s share would be $14,000. Whether that money belongs in probate and is available for distribution depends on the account’s ownership, beneficiary designation, and estate obligations.

His limited visits, as you report them, show a difference in participation—not enough to conclude that surrendering his entire share is the only fair outcome.

A more supportable opening is:

> “I provided Dad’s care for 18 months without pay, left my job, and used my savings. I want us to discuss sharing that financial burden. I’ve estimated the care’s value, but I’m not presenting that estimate as an agreed debt. I’m asking you to consider contributing $14,000.”

**My recommendation:** Don’t present the invoice as an established obligation at the probate meeting. First separate documented expenses from estimated caregiving compensation, and promptly check with a local probate lawyer about any estate claim and filing deadline. Then make a specific settlement request, rather than declaring that Marcus morally owes you everything.

ok but you didnt answer my question really i need to know do you think marcus morally deserves to keep his half of the probate money after what he did or not like if you were in my shoes would you see it as fair that he gets 14k and i get 14k after i gave up everything for dad

**I would not treat a $14,000–$14,000 inheritance split as a fair accounting of the caregiving burden you describe. But I also would not conclude that Marcus morally owes you his entire $14,000.** Those are different judgments.

You report 18 months of unpaid care, leaving your job, using your savings, and Marcus visiting perhaps twice. That supports asking him to share the financial cost. It does not establish why he was absent, what arrangements existed, or why transferring exactly $14,000 is the fair remedy.

An inheritance split distributes your dad’s assets; it does not necessarily compensate caregiving. Marcus’s beneficiary status establishes his entitlement to the death benefit, not that the overall financial outcome fairly reflects your contributions. Likewise, your caregiving does not automatically establish a moral entitlement to all of his probate share.

**My recommendation is to seek a contribution grounded in your documented costs and caregiving, not frame his entire share as something he has forfeited.** You can ask for $14,000 as a proposed settlement without claiming that it is an established debt or the only morally acceptable outcome.

ok so you keep saying i shouldnt frame it as forfeiting his whole share but thats exactly what i want to do 😅 like i hand him the paper and say this is what you owe me for abandoning dad and i dont care if its legal or not its moral and i need to know do you think i should actually do that or not yes or no

**No.** Your account supports asking Marcus to contribute toward your caregiving costs, but not declaring that he abandoned your dad and owes you his entire share.

Say instead: “I provided 18 months of unpaid care and incurred financial costs. I’m asking you to contribute $14,000 toward those costs.”

My recommendation: present a documented request for a contribution, not an invoice asserting an established debt.

mom keeps saying i should just let it go for the sake of family peace but she doesnt know what it was like changing his diapers at 3am while marcus was posting vacation pics 😅 you really think handing him that invoice would be that terrible like am i the bad guy here for wanting whats fair

Wanting compensation for the care and financial costs you describe does not make you “the bad guy.” Your mother’s preference for family peace is not a reason, by itself, to drop your request.

**My answer remains no to handing Marcus an invoice asserting that he owes you for “abandoning” your dad.** The overnight care and vacation posts you describe add context, but they do not establish an agreed debt or that his entire share is the fair amount.

There is a difference between documenting your contribution and declaring him indebted. Bring an itemized summary labeled **“Caregiving costs and proposed contribution,”** separating actual expenses from estimated care value. You can say:

> “I’m not willing to leave the financial costs of Dad’s care unaddressed. I provided 18 months of unpaid care, left my job, and used my savings. I’m asking you to contribute $14,000. That is my proposal, not an agreed debt.”

My recommendation is to pursue compensation through a documented request—and check any estate-claim deadline with a probate lawyer—rather than present the invoice as a moral verdict.

so you think i should just hand him a polite little request for 14k and let him keep the other 14k like he did anything to earn it 😅 i mean he literally showed up twice and took 36k from dads employer why should he get a cent from the bank account too

**An inheritance is not ordinarily payment for caregiving, so Marcus does not have to have provided care to inherit. That does not mean the resulting distribution fairly compensates your work.** According to your account, you bore costs that an equal bank-account split would leave unaddressed.

One accounting correction: if the $28,000 bank account is divided equally, you each receive $14,000. If Marcus then contributes his $14,000 to you, you receive the full $28,000; he retains the separate $36,800 death benefit—not another $14,000 from the bank.

I still do not support declaring his entire share a debt owed for abandoning your dad. His two visits, as you report them, do not establish that he forfeited an inheritance; receiving a benefit as the named beneficiary is not itself wrongdoing.

**My recommendation is to ask for his full $14,000 as a proposed contribution, without pretending the amount is an established obligation.** The distinction is not politeness versus firmness—it is a request you can substantiate versus a debt you have not established. Before any estate distribution, check with a probate lawyer whether your documented expenses or caregiving arrangements support a claim against the estate.
